Oklahoma's New Sweepstakes Casino Ban Takes Effect, Making Operation a Felony

Published November 14, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Oklahoma's ban on dual-currency sweepstakes casinos took effect November 1 under SB 1589, making it a felony to open, operate, or provide support services for a sweepstakes gaming platform in the state — the latest and one of the toughest moves yet in a fast-escalating, state-by-state crackdown on the sector.

What the law does

SB 1589 expanded Oklahoma's existing gambling statutes to cover online casino-style games that use virtual currencies redeemable for cash or other prizes — the core mechanic behind sweepstakes casinos like Chumba, LuckyLand, Global Poker, and Stake.us, which let players use free "Gold Coin" currency for fun while a parallel "Sweeps Coin" currency can be redeemed for real cash prizes. Under the new law, opening, conducting, working for, or providing support for that kind of platform is a Class C2 felony, with fines reported between $500 and $2,000 attached to the bill. The law doesn't stop at operators: it also reaches geolocation providers, gaming suppliers, platform providers, promoters, and media affiliates that support a prohibited platform.

Governor Kevin Stitt vetoed the bill in May, warning that it "criminalizes everyday apps people use for fun" and "unnecessarily creates a new felony and extends criminal liability to businesses and service providers." The legislature overrode his veto anyway, by a 34-10 vote in the Senate and a 68-19 vote in the House.

Part of a broader pattern nationally

Oklahoma is the latest state to move against sweepstakes casinos, but the approaches vary. Florida's attorney general sued VGW and Stake back in August under existing deceptive-trade-practices and gambling law, without needing new legislation, and followed up by sending Google, Meta, Reddit, Snap, and TikTok letters demanding they stop carrying ads for sweepstakes platforms. Pennsylvania has a bill pending in its House Gaming Oversight Committee that would impose fines of $50,000 to $500,000 per violation, though it hasn't had a hearing and the session ends November 30. Wyoming's legislature has also been drafting its own restrictions, with one competing proposal that would have allowed regulated sweepstakes casinos under stricter consumer protections instead of banning them outright, though that version reportedly failed to advance.

The Social Gaming Leadership Alliance, a trade group representing sweepstakes operators, has pushed back on the outright-ban approach. Its executive director, Sean Ostrow, argued that "outright bans aren't effective deterrents and certainly don't curb consumer demands," and said the group would rather see registration requirements and know-your-customer rules than prohibition. For players, the practical effect is the same regardless of which side is right about policy: platforms operating in increasingly contested legal territory carry real risk of disrupted access, frozen balances, or a sudden shutdown with little warning — one more reason our own casino guides stick to games offered through standard, licensed real-money frameworks.
